title: Book 02 — Chapter 8, Part 2: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 8, Part 2: The Promised [Maw‘ud] al-Mahdi
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Each question and model answer was checked against the original Al-Islam.org chapter. Historical claims are attributed to Mutahhari or to the report he cites; interpretive conclusions are distinguished from reported events.

revision_policy: Exam-ready model answers, not answer fragments.
Use the author’s actual distinctions and examples; do not overstate reports as independently established facts.
The answer is written so it can be reproduced in an examination, with the reasoning made explicit.
Question types include recall, explanation, evidence, comparison, application, and synthesis.

questions.prompt: What is the central historical question Mutahhari sets out to examine in this lecture, and how does it differ from merely proving the doctrine from texts?
questions.answer: Mutahhari asks when belief in the Promised al-Mahdi began and what effect that belief had on Islamic history. He acknowledges Qur’anic verses and Prophetic reports, but says he does not intend to examine those narrations in detail in this lecture. Instead, he traces historical events that occurred because people already knew of the promised Mahdi: political movements, pledges of allegiance, disputed claims, and the reactions of scholars and rulers. The distinction is important: the lecture is primarily a historical investigation into the doctrine’s presence and influence, not a complete hadith-authentication study or a full proof of every doctrinal detail.

questions.prompt: Which Qur’anic passages does Mutahhari use to establish the broad promise of the righteous inheriting the earth, and what scope does he draw from them?
questions.answer: Mutahhari refers especially to Qur’an 21:105, which states that the righteous servants will inherit the earth, and Qur’an 9:33, which speaks of the religion of truth prevailing over other religions. He interprets these promises as universal rather than limited to one city, nation, race, or geographical region. The earth will not remain permanently under oppressive rulers; the righteous will ultimately inherit it. He connects this Qur’anic horizon with the promised al-Mahdi. In an exam, distinguish the Qur’anic wording from Mutahhari’s interpretation: the verses provide the scriptural basis, while his lecture explains their future-oriented and universal significance.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari consider the presence of Sunni narrations about the Mahdi important to his argument?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that if the Prophet had spoken about the Promised Mahdi, the reports should not be confined to Shi‘ah transmission. He therefore points to Sunni narrations and to works that collect them, including the Arabic book al-Mahdi by Ayatullah Sadr and Muntakhab al-Athar by Ayatullah Safi Golpaygani, which also cites many Sunni traditions. This cross-sectarian evidence supports his claim that belief in the Mahdi was not invented only by Shi‘ahs in the third century AH. The point is about the breadth and early circulation of the expectation; it does not mean that every Sunni and Shi‘ah report has identical wording, grading, or interpretation.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of Imam ‘Ali’s statement to Kumayl that the earth is never empty of Allah’s proof.
questions.answer: In the account quoted by Mutahhari, Imam ‘Ali tells Kumayl that humanity includes the learned, those seeking knowledge, and the ignorant, and laments the scarcity of worthy people to receive his knowledge. He then affirms that the earth is never empty of Allah’s proof: the proof may be manifest and publicly known, or hidden and concealed from people’s sight. Mutahhari uses this statement to show that the idea of a divine proof who may be concealed was present in material attributed to Imam ‘Ali, long before the birth of Imam al-Mahdi in the third century AH. The statement supports the continuity of the idea, rather than by itself identifying every historical detail of the later Imam’s life.

questions.prompt: How did Mukhtar use the belief in the Promised Mahdi to strengthen his political position, and what does Mutahhari leave undecided?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says Mukhtar sought support for his campaign to avenge the killing of Imam al-Husayn, but people were reluctant to accept his leadership. Mukhtar therefore presented Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah, Imam ‘Ali’s son and Imam al-Husayn’s brother, as the Promised Mahdi, reasoning from the report that the Mahdi would share the Prophet’s name. Mukhtar then described himself as the Mahdi’s representative. Mutahhari explicitly declines to judge whether Mukhtar was good or evil and says that Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah’s own acceptance of the identification is not proven. The exam answer must therefore separate Mukhtar’s political use of the claim from what can be established about Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah’s personal belief.

questions.prompt: What happened after Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah died, and how did this contribute to the emergence of the Hanafiyyah idea?
questions.answer: After Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah’s death, some followers refused to accept that he had died, because they believed the Promised Mahdi would not die before filling the earth with justice. They claimed that he was concealed in Mount Radwa. Mutahhari identifies this development with the later emergence of the Hanafiyyah idea. The episode illustrates how an established expectation of the Mahdi could shape the interpretation of a leader’s death: instead of revising their identification, followers interpreted the death as concealment. It is an example of a historical claim made by followers, not proof that Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah was in fact the promised Imam.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari draw from Zuhri’s reaction to the martyrdom of Zayd ibn ‘Ali?
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites a report from Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani’s Maqatil al-Talibiyyin, a work by a historian he identifies as non-Shi‘ah. When Zuhri heard of Zayd ibn ‘Ali’s martyrdom, he reportedly remarked that the Ahl al-Bayt should not rush, because the day when the Mahdi would emerge from them would come. Mutahhari’s purpose is not to endorse Zuhri’s criticism of Zayd’s uprising; he explicitly says that is not his concern. He uses the remark as evidence that expectation of a future Mahdi from the Prophet’s Household was familiar beyond Shi‘ah circles. The source and the author’s limited inference should both be stated.

questions.prompt: Who was Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, known as Nafs Zakiyyah, and why did people identify him with the Mahdi?
questions.answer: Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah was the son of ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, who was descended from Imam al-Hasan through his father and from Imam al-Husayn through his mother, Fatimah bint al-Husayn. The title al-Mahd described his pure Alawi and Fatimi lineage. Muhammad became known as Nafs Zakiyyah and attracted support near the end of the Umayyad period. People associated him with the promised Mahdi partly because he shared the Prophet’s name and was reported to have a mark on his shoulder resembling the Prophet’s Seal of Prophethood. Mutahhari explains how these signs and the widespread expectation encouraged people to pledge allegiance to him under the title of the Mahdi.

questions.prompt: How did Imam al-Sadiq distinguish support for a righteous uprising from accepting Nafs Zakiyyah as the Promised Mahdi?
questions.answer: When invited to pledge allegiance to Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, Imam al-Sadiq asked what the uprising intended to achieve. He said he would support Muhammad if the purpose was to enjoin good and forbid evil. However, if Muhammad was claiming to be the Promised Mahdi, Imam al-Sadiq rejected that identification and said that the promised figure was someone else. This distinction is central: approval of a just cause or moral reform does not automatically validate a claimant’s identity as the divinely promised Mahdi. Mutahhari uses the episode to show that the existence of a widespread belief did not remove the need to examine a particular claimant’s claim.

questions.prompt: What example does Mutahhari give of Mansur’s political exploitation of the title al-Mahdi?
questions.answer: Mutahhari reports that the Abbasid caliph Mansur named his son al-Mahdi and that historians described this as a political attempt to appropriate the public expectation of the Promised Mahdi. The lecture recounts that Mansur allegedly told different audiences contradictory things: privately, he could say that neither his son nor ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd was the promised figure, while publicly he could present his own son as the Mahdi. Mutahhari’s point is that a religious expectation with strong public influence could be manipulated for dynastic legitimacy. These are historical reports cited by the author; an accurate answer attributes the account to Mutahhari rather than claiming direct access to Mansur’s private intentions.

questions.prompt: Who was Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan, why did he pledge allegiance to ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, and how was he saved from punishment?
questions.answer: Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan was a Medinan scholar who pledged allegiance to ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd because he believed him to be the Promised Mahdi. Mansur treated the pledge as allegiance to a political enemy and ordered that Ibn ‘Ijlan’s hands be cut off. Medinan scholars intervened, explaining that Ibn ‘Ijlan was a learned man who acted on a mistaken religious identification, not out of hostility toward the Abbasid ruler. Mutahhari recounts the episode to show that belief in the Mahdi had concrete political consequences and could lead people to take serious risks. It also demonstrates the danger of accepting a claimant without careful investigation.

questions.prompt: Why did Imam al-Sadiq publicly display the body of his son Isma‘il, according to Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari recounts that Isma‘il died while Imam al-Sadiq was still alive. At the funeral, the Imam repeatedly showed Isma‘il’s face and asked witnesses to recognize that he had died. The purpose, as Mutahhari explains it, was to prevent people from later claiming that Isma‘il had not died but had disappeared as the Promised Mahdi. The episode shows that mistaken identifications could arise even around the family of an Imam, and that the Imam took deliberate steps to prevent such confusion. It should be described as the author’s account of the Imam’s intention, not generalized beyond what the text states.

questions.prompt: What role does Di‘bil’s lamentation before Imam al-Rida play in Mutahhari’s historical argument?
questions.answer: Di‘bil recited a lamentation recalling the sufferings and martyrdoms of members of the Ahl al-Bayt. When the poem referred to graves associated with the family, Imam al-Rida added a line about a grave in Tus and explained that it would be his own. Mutahhari also notes that Di‘bil’s poetry connected the history of suffering with the eventual reappearance of an Imam. The episode links remembrance of past oppression with hope for future justice. It supports Mutahhari’s broader claim that Mahdism was woven into the religious consciousness of Muslims and was not merely a doctrine introduced at the birth of Imam al-Mahdi.

questions.prompt: What is the distinction between the widespread belief in the Mahdi and the repeated appearance of false claimants?
questions.answer: Mutahhari distinguishes the existence of a general expectation of a promised Mahdi from the correctness of identifying any particular person as that figure. He cites claimants and movements across different periods and regions to show that the belief had broad influence. But the fact that people repeatedly claimed the title—or that followers mistakenly accepted someone—does not establish that the claimant was authentic. Indeed, the history of mistaken identifications demonstrates why evidence and careful examination are necessary. The existence of impostors does not, by itself, disprove the underlying expectation; it shows that a powerful religious belief can be exploited or misunderstood.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari infer from references to Mahdism in poems attributed to Hafiz, and what qualification does he make?
questions.answer: Mutahhari points to Mahdist imagery in poems attributed to Hafiz as evidence that the expectation of a rescuer and the Mahdi had a place in Persian literary culture. However, he explicitly says that he cannot establish whether Hafiz was Shi‘ah or Sunni and that one should not claim certainty about the poet’s sect. The example therefore supports the cultural reach of Mahdist imagery, not a definitive conclusion about Hafiz’s personal doctrinal affiliation. This qualification is important because Mutahhari distinguishes what a text can show—the presence of a theme—from what it cannot establish—the author’s precise religious identity.

questions.prompt: Trace the historical evidence Mutahhari presents to argue that belief in the Promised Mahdi did not originate only in the third century AH.
questions.answer: Mutahhari’s argument proceeds through a sequence of Qur’anic, transmitted, and historical evidence. First, he points to Qur’anic promises that the righteous will inherit the earth and that the religion of truth will ultimately prevail. Second, he notes that reports about the Mahdi are found in Sunni as well as Shi‘ah sources, so the expectation cannot be dismissed as a late, exclusively Shi‘ah invention. Third, he cites Imam ‘Ali’s statement to Kumayl that the earth is never empty of Allah’s proof, whether manifest or concealed. He then turns to historical examples: Mukhtar’s identification of Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah; Zuhri’s reported expectation of a future Mahdi from the Ahl al-Bayt; the identification of Nafs Zakiyyah; Mansur’s political use of the title; Ibn ‘Ijlan’s pledge; Imam al-Sadiq’s public demonstration of Isma‘il’s death; and Di‘bil’s poetry before Imam al-Rida. Finally, he points to Sunni Mahdist movements and Mahdist imagery in Hafiz. Together, these examples show that the expectation had a history and influence before the birth of Imam al-Mahdi. They do not make every claimant authentic; rather, they establish the antiquity and historical force of the belief.

questions.prompt: Compare the cases of Mukhtar, Nafs Zakiyyah, Mansur, and Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan. What do they reveal about the political consequences of Mahdist belief?
questions.answer: The four cases show different ways in which belief in the Mahdi could shape political conduct. Mukhtar used the expectation to strengthen his campaign by presenting Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the promised figure and himself as the Mahdi’s representative. Nafs Zakiyyah attracted allegiance partly because people associated his lineage, name, and reported physical sign with the expected Mahdi, although Imam al-Sadiq distinguished support for a righteous uprising from accepting that identification. Mansur, by contrast, is portrayed as manipulating the title for Abbasid legitimacy, even making contradictory claims about who the Mahdi was. Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan represents a follower who pledged allegiance to ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd because he sincerely believed him to be the promised figure, and was nearly punished for it. The comparison shows that Mahdist belief could inspire movements, attract allegiance, be exploited by rulers, and expose sincere believers to danger. Mutahhari’s central caution is that widespread expectation must not replace critical examination of a claimant.

questions.prompt: Explain why the historical examples of mistaken Mahdi claimants do not, in Mutahhari’s argument, disprove the belief in the Promised Mahdi.
questions.answer: Mutahhari separates a general doctrine from the claims made by particular individuals or their followers. The fact that people identified Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah, Nafs Zakiyyah, or other figures as the Mahdi does not mean that each identification was correct. Rather, the repeated attempts to identify a claimant show that the expectation was already widely known and influential. False or mistaken claimants are therefore evidence of the belief’s social and political force, not a logical refutation of the belief itself. The correct method is to assess the underlying doctrine and the evidence for a specific claimant separately. Mutahhari also emphasizes that early disagreements often concerned which person was the Mahdi, rather than whether a promised Mahdi existed at all. A strong answer must avoid the fallacy of treating the failure of one claimant as proof that the general expectation is false.

questions.prompt: What two interpretations of social change does Mutahhari compare when discussing the conditions for the Mahdi’s reappearance? Explain why he prefers the image of ripening fruit to an abscess bursting.
questions.answer: Mutahhari contrasts a revolutionary model based on explosion with a model based on gradual maturation. In the first model, corruption is like an abscess: it must accumulate until it bursts, so reform is treated as an obstacle and people may even welcome worsening disorder. Mutahhari rejects applying this model to the Mahdi’s reappearance because it would imply opposing reform and allowing sin to spread. He instead says the reappearance is more like a fruit ripening. A fruit becomes ready when it reaches the necessary maturity; similarly, the world must attain a certain level of competence and develop worthy people capable of supporting a just government. The point is not that society must become morally perfect or that every historical change is orderly. It is that believers must not deliberately produce corruption. They should contribute to moral and social development while awaiting the promised transformation.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari reject the idea that believers should oppose reform or allow corruption to increase in order to hasten the reappearance?
questions.answer: Mutahhari rejects this view because it turns a promise of future justice into an excuse for present wrongdoing. Some people reason that if universal justice comes after the world is filled with oppression, then reform must be resisted and corruption allowed to grow. Mutahhari asks whether this would mean abandoning prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, enjoining good, forbidding evil, and educating children. He answers emphatically that awaiting the Imam invalidates none of the personal or social duties imposed by Islam. Reform, religious education, worship, and public moral responsibility are not obstacles to reappearance; he says such efforts can help bring it closer. Therefore, the believer must not manufacture the evil that the promised Imam is expected to overcome. Genuine waiting requires action, discipline, and preparation—not passivity or deliberate corruption.

questions.prompt: Explain Mutahhari’s understanding of Mahdism as a global philosophy rather than a narrowly sectarian or national hope.
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that Mahdism must not be reduced to the hope that one particular nation or sect will gain power or enjoy prosperity. He reads the Qur’anic promise that the righteous will inherit the earth as universal in scope: it concerns the earth, not one region or race. The promised future is a transformation of human society in which wisdom, justice, spirituality, and moral maturity replace domination by ignorance, rage, lust, and oppression. He presents human history by analogy with the stages of an individual’s life: childhood, youth, and maturity. Humanity, too, must move beyond a stage dominated by myths and ignorance and a stage in which knowledge is still governed by aggression and desire, toward a mature age ruled by wisdom. Mahdism is therefore a philosophy of hope for the future of humanity as a whole, and it should shape believers’ conduct through responsibility and moral preparation.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari say about the disagreements that arose after the deaths of some of the Imams, and what does he identify as the main point of disagreement?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that after the deaths of several Imams, some groups claimed that the Imam had not really died but had disappeared and was the Promised Mahdi. He mentions cases associated with Imam al-Baqir, Imam al-Kazim, Imam al-Sadiq, and others. He then makes an important distinction: in his reading of the historical record, the main disagreement was generally not whether a Promised Mahdi would appear, but which individual was that Mahdi. Questions included whether he was the son of Imam al-Hasan al-‘Askari, whether he belonged to the descendants of Imam al-Hasan or Imam al-Husayn, and whether a particular Imam who had died was actually concealed. Mutahhari says that, as far as his research indicated, scholars up to Ibn Khaldun accepted the basis of the narrations, while disputes concerned identification and details. Present this as Mutahhari’s summary of the record, not as an independently exhaustive survey of every scholar.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari’s footnote about Zayd ibn ‘Ali qualify the report of Zuhri’s reaction to Zayd’s martyrdom?
questions.answer: Mutahhari’s main text reports Zuhri as asking why the Ahl al-Bayt were rushing into rebellion when the day of the Mahdi’s emergence from among them would come. Mutahhari says that he is not assessing the validity of Zuhri’s objection; he uses the remark as evidence that expectation of a future Mahdi from the Prophet’s Household was familiar. The footnote then adds an important qualification from the Shi‘ah perspective: Zayd is described as a righteous and pious person, and the Imams’ reports praise him. According to the narrations cited there, Zayd’s uprising was for enjoining good and forbidding evil, not for claiming the Imamate. Therefore, the report should not be used to imply that Zayd himself claimed to be the Mahdi or that his uprising was a claim to the Imamate.

questions.prompt: What does footnote 5 clarify about the Prophet’s early statement concerning the Mahdi, and why is that clarification important?
questions.answer: Footnote 5 explains that the Prophet’s early statement, as presented in the chapter, was that a Mahdi from his descendants would definitely reappear. It did not specify the time of reappearance in historical terms. Mutahhari adds that a select group may have known whose son the promised figure would be, but the public statement itself did not provide a detailed timetable or all the later identifying particulars. This clarification matters because it prevents readers from projecting later historical details backward into the earliest reports. It also helps explain why the general expectation could be widely known while disagreements later arose over the identity of particular claimants. In an exam, distinguish the broad Prophetic promise from later debates about the person, lineage, and timing.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari connect the historical survey of Mahdism with the practical duty of awaiting the Imam?
questions.answer: Mutahhari first establishes that expectation of the Mahdi was present in Qur’anic promises, reports, statements attributed to Imam ‘Ali, and historical events across Muslim society. He then turns from the history of the belief to its ethical consequences. If the promised future is one of justice, believers must not interpret the prophecy as permission to tolerate or create injustice in the present. He rejects passive waiting and the claim that religious obligations should be abandoned to make society worse. Instead, prayer, fasting, charity, Hajj, education, enjoining good, forbidding evil, writing, teaching, and social reform remain duties. The final vision is global: the future belongs to a mature humanity governed by wisdom, justice, and spirituality. Thus, historical belief should produce hope and responsibility. The stronger the conviction in a just future, the more meaningful present moral preparation becomes.

questions.prompt: According to the report cited by Mutahhari, what did Imam ‘Ali tell Kumayl about the earth and Allah’s proof?
questions.answer: The earth is never empty of Allah’s proof, whether manifest or concealed.
options: The earth is never empty of Allah’s proof, whether manifest or concealed.
The proof must always be a publicly ruling political leader.
The proof disappears whenever people reject the Imams.
The earth is guided only by written books, never by a living proof.

questions.prompt: What distinction did Imam al-Sadiq make regarding Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd?
questions.answer: He could support an uprising for enjoining good and forbidding evil, but he rejected identifying Muhammad as the Promised Mahdi.
options: He could support an uprising for enjoining good and forbidding evil, but he rejected identifying Muhammad as the Promised Mahdi.
He rejected every form of social reform and political action.
He accepted Muhammad as the Promised Mahdi but opposed his methods.
He said that no descendant of Imam al-Hasan could ever lead an uprising.
